The Fintech Brief Il

Analysing the success of the Uk’s fintech industry

The UK’s fintech industry is driving global change in 
traditional banking, payment, and lending services. The 
sector has seen meteoric growth since our records began in 
2011, with an astonishing £2.4b of funding deployed over 
210 rounds in 2019. 
The outbreak of coronavirus, and the economic 
uncertainty that has accompanied it, has threatened this 
upwards trend. Still, fintech is better positioned than most 
to weather the storm, and has maintained its position as 
the UK’s strongest high-growth sector.
Almost seven months on from the start of lockdown, we’ve 
evaluated the current state of the market and the factors 
that contribute to its success. Alongside the geographical 
distribution of companies, we provide an update on 
fundraising statistics, and conclude with our ranking of the 
five most ambitious UK fintech companies.
Introduction

What do we mean by 
ambitious? 
We use eight criteria to identify high-growth and 
ambitious companies. 
Each of these is a sign of external validation that a 
business is either actively growing or creating ambitious 
growth plans. 
All companies featured in this report have met at least one 
of these growth triggers. 
Equity investment
Accelerator attendance
Scaleups
MBO/MBI
Venture debt
Grant recipients
High-growth lists
Academic spinouts

There are currently 1,005 active, ambitious fintech 
companies in the UK. That’s around 3% of all high-growth 
UK businesses. 
Over the past 18 months, the number of high-growth UK 
fintechs has increased by around a third, as the industry 
continues to expand at a rapid rate. 
An impressive 105 fintechs have exited the market, either 
through an IPO or acquisition, and 208 are no longer 
trading. 
Fintech is a young sector, with 35% of companies at seed 
stage, and 27% at venture stage. This compares with just 
30% and 15%, respectively, in the high-growth sector as a 
whole. 
Stages of evolution
Current stages of evolution of UK fintechs

Geography
London is widely considered as the fintech capital of 
Europe, and the density of companies found there is 
testament to this. An impressive 806 high-growth fintechs 
reside in the city, representing 73% of all those in the UK. 
This proportion has remained largely unchanged in recent 
years. But whilst the Capital is still dominant in UK 
fintech, it doesn’t hold a monopoly.
There are fintech clusters thriving across the country, 
most notably in Bristol, Manchester and Edinburgh. The 
high-growth ecosystems in these regions are continuing 
to draw ambitious fintech companies to the area. 
Geographical 
distribution  of 
active fintech 
companies

Methods of growth
There are a variety of ways in which fintech companies can 
grow and fuel their ambitions. Several have used 
accelerator programmes to launch themselves into the 
next stage of growth. We’ve tracked 439 accelerator 
attendances by UK fintechs since 2011. 
Meanwhile, just 10 of the UK’s high-growth fintechs have 
been spun-out of a university. Spin-outs benefit from 
intensive research and development, as well as extended 
support from the institutions they’re born out of. 
Equity investment, however, is by far the most popular 
method of growth amongst UK fintechs. And they have 
their pick of funds to choose from. Investors from all over 
the world look to the UK for high-potential fintech 
opportunities. The inflow of capital, combined with the 
expertise of investors, helps elevate these businesses to 
reach new markets and expand their oﬀering.

UK fintech has seen a sustained period of growth in the 
number of equity fundraisings since 2011. 
Between Q1 2011 and Q3 2020, fintech companies have 
secured 1,234 publicly announced equity deals, worth 
£9.82b in total. The average value of these investments 
was £8.45m.
2019 was a record year for fintech, with 210 equity deals 
worth a combined £2.4b. That’s £800m more than the year 
prior. 
It seems there’s an ever-increasing amount of capital 
available to support UK fintech companies right now, 
which is playing a major part in the industry’s growth.
Fundraisings: big picture
Number and value of announced equity deals into UK fintechs 
Q1 2011 - Q3 2020

In 2019, there was significant variation in the amount of 
capital invested in each quarter, from £1b in Q1 to just 
£328m in Q4. The number of deals completed also 
fluctuated, between 42 in Q3 and 62 in Q4. 
2020 started oﬀ strong, with £1b worth of equity invested 
over 55 deals in Q1. But in the midst of a national 
lockdown, there was a dramatic drop in the value of 
investments. Just £375m was invested in Q2 2020, 
compared to £680m in Q2 2019. 
Still, more pounds were invested than in Q4 2019, and 
more deals completed than in Q3 2019. Q3 2020 was also 
strong, with 47 rounds totalling £984m—more than double 
Q3 2019. Is this a sign of positive recovery or a mass 
bail-out? Our data suggests the former: 95% of fintechs 
have avoided the worst eﬀects of the pandemic.
Fundraisings: 2019-2020
Number and value of announced equity deals into UK fintechs 
Q1 2019 - Q3 2020

Despite making up the largest proportion of fintechs, fewer 
seed stage deals are happening each year. As we’ve been 
warning for a couple of years now, this is a worrying sign. If 
seed-stage activity continues to drop oﬀ, the pipeline of 
investable companies at later stages will diminish over time.
Generally, companies in traditional sectors have already 
reached profitability by the established stage of growth, and 
may not need further funding. But in such a young and 
competitive industry, fintechs often follow a ‘growth before 
profit’ model, and may still rely on equity at this stage. 
Revolut, Zopa and Starling Bank are all examples of 
loss-making businesses that have raised huge sums in the 
established stage of growth. Currently, just 3% of fintech 
deals have been completed at the established stage, but we 
expect this proportion to increase over the coming years, 
and at a faster rate than other sectors. 
Fundraisings: by stage 
Number of announced equity deals into UK fintechs by stage
Q1 2019 - Q3 2020

Alongside a very healthy collection of sector agnostic 
investors, the UK is also home to a number of 
fintech-focused funds. 
These range from venture capital firms to corporate 
venturing arms, and early stage finance to growth stage 
capital. 
As experts in the fintech space, these funds can oﬀer 
ongoing mentoring and sector-specific advice to their 
portfolio companies. 
We currently track seven UK funds that exclusively invest in 
fintech companies, and a further 30 that list fintech as one 
of their preferred sectors of operation.
Dedicated investors
Mouro Capital
Spunout from Santander InnoVentures, Mouro 
Capital is now an autonomous London-based VC 
firm with $400m assets under management that 
invests in early to growth stage fintechs.
FinTech Circle
Based in Barnet, FinTech Circle is Europe’s first 
fintech-focused angel network. After a rigorous 
application process, founders pitch to investors, 
who collectively oﬀer between £70k and £500k. 
Augmentum Fintech
Augmentum Fintech is a patient VC fund that 
invests across Europe. Its portfolio companies 
have unique or disruptive business models and a 
first mover advantage.
Outward VC
Backed by Investec, Outward VC invests in early 
stage fintechs addressing global opportunities. As 
long-term investors, the majority of the firm’s  
funds are reserved for follow-on.

Accelerator programmes are all about getting a company 
oﬀ the ground and giving them the tools they need to 
realise their full potential. 
The number of these programmes has grown 
dramatically in the last few years, with many now 
specialising in specific verticals like fintech. 
We currently track seven fintech-focused accelerators, as 
well as a further 26 more general tech programmes.
Collectively, 188 high-growth UK companies have 
attended fintech-specific accelerators. These include 
ambitious businesses like 9fin, PrimaryBid, Aire, 
GoodBox, and Flux.

With an impressive 641% growth in turnover, Monzo is the fastest-growing 
fintech in the country. Monzo oﬀers customers a range of banking and money 
management services via its app. Users can track and budget their money, 
access loans, or open savings accounts instantly.  
To date, Monzo has received £384m in fundraisings, through 12 rounds of 
investment. It has also attended two of Tech Nation’s accelerator programmes 
(Future Fifty and Upscale), and been named on several high-growth lists, most 
recently The FinTech50. 
In June, after the closure of its Las Vegas oﬀice, Monzo announced 120 UK 
redundancies. And in its most recent round of fundraising, the company took a 
40% reduction in its valuation. Even still, Monzo’s app continues to be used by 
over 4m people. 
 1     Monzo  
Location:  London (Liverpool St)
Stage of evolution:  Growth 
Employees:  >1000
2019 turnover:  £19.7m
Growth from previous:  641%

In second place, with 229% growth in turnover between 2018 and 2019, is 
Habito―the free digital mortgage brokerage, and now lender, which allows 
users to compare, apply for, and track their mortgages online. 
To date, Habito has received £83.3m in fundraisings, through five rounds of 
investment. It also joins Monzo on this year’s The FinTech50 high-growth list. 
The company currently has a potentially positive COVID-19 impact status, 
meaning it can potentially grow its operations as a result of the pandemic. 
Habito recently became one of 3,500 Certified B Corp companies committed 
to putting “people and planet on the same level as profit”, alongside big 
names like Ben & Jerry’s and Patagonia.
 2     Habito  
Location:  London (Whitechapel)
Stage of evolution:  Growth 
Employees:  100-249
2019 turnover:  £2.72m
Growth from previous:  229%

Close behind Habito, with 224% growth in turnover, Bibimoney is relatively 
new to the scene—hitting our tracking triggers for the first time in August. 
The company’s innovative technology provides secure mobile wallet services 
that work on any phone and any mobile network. Users can transfer money 
and make payments from their digital wallets, with no WiFi or data required.
Through its pioneering product, Bibimoney is hoping to support global 
development by increasing financial inclusion for the unbanked and 
underbanked. Its working with the UK Government, NGOs, and the UN, and 
has established partnerships around the world. 
To date, the company has raised £788k in fundraisings, through two rounds of 
investment. Its current COVID-19 impact status is set to low.
 3     Bibimoney  
Location:  London (Islington)
Stage of evolution:  Venture 
Employees:  5-9
2019 turnover:  £1.1m
Growth from previous:  224%

Next up, with 197% growth in turnover, is the travel, restaurant, and event 
recommendation app, Velocity Black. 
Using a mix of human and machine power, Velocity Black claims to be the 
ultimate members club, “reimagined for the digital age”. The app enables its 
members to book and pay for everything through their phones.
To date, Velocity has received £32.8m in fundraisings, through seven rounds of 
investment. It’s also a member of the 2019 Forbes Technology Council, and its 
app has members in over 60 countries.
Despite being classed as severely impacted in June, Velocity’s COVID-19 
impact status has improved significantly, and is currently set to potentially 
positive.
 4     Velocity  
Location:  London (Westminster)
Stage of evolution:  Growth 
Employees:  50-99
2019 turnover:  £7.82m
Growth from previous:  197%

Fifth in our ranking, with 194% growth in turnover, is the company trying to 
make banking “10x better”. 10x has developed an open banking platform for 
the financial services industry. 
Founded in 2016 by Antony Jenkins, former Group CEO of Barclays, 10x aims 
to improve customer experience for banks. The company uses its cloud-native 
platform to provide more timely, relevant, and personalised experiences for 
its clients’ customers.
To date, 10x has raised £89.9m in fundraisings through three rounds of 
investment. And, like several of the fintech companies in our ranking, its 
COVID-19 impact status is currently set to potentially positive. 
 5     10x Banking  
Location:  London (Westminster)
Stage of evolution:  Growth 
Employees:  100-249
2019 turnover:  £54.7m
Growth from previous:  194%
